newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine to cut gas consumption, revamp system.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine to cut gas consumption, revamp system.

text.p: Ukraine, the biggest consumer of Russian gas, plans to reduce gas consumption and modernise its private distribution system, leading industry officials said on Thursday.
Mykhailo Kovalko, head of the State Oil and Gas Committee, told Ukrainian radio on Thursday that Ukraine's goal was to cut Russian gas imports by 20 percent over an unspecified period.
"Ukraine aims to reach gas consumption of 76 billion cubic metres (bcm) in 1998," Kovalko said. "There is already a clear tendency in reducing gas consumption in Ukraine."
Prime Minister Valery Pustovoitenko told a news conference on Wednesday that plans called for 75 bcm next year compared to 80 bcm in 1996.

Ukraine is due to import 53 bcm of Russian gas this year, of which about 32 bcm would be in the form of payments from Russian gas monopoly Gazprom for transit of some 125 bcm of Russian gas to Europe via Ukrainian territory.
Kiev also is due to get up to 20 bcm of gas from the central Asian states of Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
Pustovoitenko said the government planned to keep stable domestic gas output at 18 bcm, despite fears by energy officials that Ukraine lacked funds to develop its deposits.

A government group, chaired by deputy prime ministers Anatoly Holubchenko and Serhiy Tyhypko, has been working since last month on a new, more competetive gas distribution scheme which in 1995 was handed to several private gas traders.
Pustovoitenko said there would be tenders for rights to distribute gas and traders would be obliged to pay for licenses, from which Ukraine hopes to raise $1 billion in fees.
Pustovoitenko, who last month replaced Pavlo Lazarenko -- creator and advocate of the gas scheme -- accused gas traders of pocketing profits and converting foreign into domestic debt.
"The gas complex worked badly and gave a chance for some people to make money," Pustovoitenko said.

"I cannot understand those people who fly (their own) planes while Ukrainian people have not been paid for eight months," he added, referring to Ukraine's debt of 6.7 billion hryvnias ($3.6 billion) for wages, pensions and student grants.
Pustovoitenko said the government did not want to "push out some traders from the market" but wanted to establish order.

The former president of country's biggest gas trader United Energy Systems of Ukraine (UES), parliamentary deputy Yulia Tymoshenko, last week accused the government and presidential administration of destabilising Ukraine's gas market.

"The official gas policy is on the brink of being criminal," Tymoshenko told Moscow's Nezavisimaya Gazeta last week, adding that Ukraine's problem was many budget-funded, state-owned enterprises not paying their gas bills.
Last month Kuchma and Gazprom's chief Rem Vyakhirev agreed the private distribution scheme would remain for at least 1998 despite some defects.

"Gas traders were not guilty for sometimes overstepping legal boundaries. They simply used the situation to their advantage," Kuchma's representative to parliament Ivan Bezsmertny said on Thursday. "But the energy market cannot exist without some rules of the game."
